title: Which radio and which software should I pick for an MSPM0 or CC23xx board?
short: For a battery sensor that talks to a phone, pick Bluetooth LE. For a smart home you already run with a hub, pick Zigbee or Thread. For Apple Home, Google Home or Alexa, pick Matter, which runs over Thread or Wi-Fi. Pick Wi-Fi when the device is plugged in, and Sub-1 GHz when it is far from the house. For software, TI's SDK has the radio stacks and TI's compiler. On CoreMark at -O3 that compiler was 26 percent faster than GCC: 2.30 against 1.82 per MHz on the LP-MSPM0G3507. Zephyr lets the same code move between chips and vendors. With the same GCC compiler it cost us 4 to 8 percent on one LP-MSPM0G3507. The C library also differs.

questions.q: What is already in your house?

answers.t: A Zigbee hub or a USB Zigbee radio
A Thread border router, listed below

ble.name: Bluetooth LE
ble.why: It sleeps on very little power and talks to a phone directly, or to Home Assistant through a Bluetooth adapter or an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy.

zigbee.name: Zigbee
zigbee.why: Your hub already speaks it, and battery sensors last on it.

thread.name: Thread
thread.why: Low power like Zigbee, with internet-style addresses, through the border router you have.

matter.name: Matter, over Thread or Wi-Fi
matter.why: One device works in Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant at once. On a battery that means Matter over Thread, which needs a Thread border router; plugged in, Matter over Wi-Fi needs no extra box.

wifi.name: Wi-Fi
wifi.why: Plugged in, it joins your network directly with no extra box.

long.name: Sub-1 GHz long range
long.why: It reaches farther and gets through walls better than 2.4 GHz radios.

glance_intro: Matter is not on this table because it is not a radio. It runs over Thread or Wi-Fi, covered in the next section. Power figures come from data sheets at different voltages and power levels, so compare sizes and ignore exact ratios. Range depends on your walls more than the radio. 1 kB = 1,024 bytes.

matter_explainer: Matter is not a radio. It is a common language for smart-home devices, from the Connectivity Standards Alliance, that runs on IP networks: Wi-Fi, Thread or Ethernet. Bluetooth LE only sets a new device up. So you choose between Matter over Thread, which is low power and needs a border router, and Matter over Wi-Fi, which needs no extra box and uses more power. One Matter device can sit in Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa and Home Assistant at once. Matter needs a big part. TI marks Matter over Thread on the CC2755P10 as evaluation, and Matter over Wi-Fi on the CC3551E as production. The CC3551E board is the LP-EM-CC35X1. TI offers no Matter build for the CC2340R5.

radios.name: Bluetooth LE
radios.one: Talks straight to a phone or computer, no hub. A CC2340R5 sleeps at 0.71 µA between radio events (data sheet).
pick_when: A phone app should talk to it directly
It runs for a long time on a coin cell
You want readings in Home Assistant through a Bluetooth adapter or an ESPHome Bluetooth proxy (BTHome is an open format it reads)
skip_when: Messages need to hop across the house through other devices: Zigbee and Thread do that by default
It should appear in Apple Home or Google Home on its own: use Matter
facts: 5.1 to 10.7 mA sending, 0.71 µA asleep (CC2340R5 data sheet, 3.0 V)
No IP address; a phone or hub talks to it
radios.measured: LP-EM-CC2340R5: on air 1.40 s after flashing, connects to a Mac in 0.55 s, 45 ms round trip for 20 bytes.

radios.name: Zigbee
radios.one: A low-power mesh for lights, plugs and sensors, run by a hub. Mains-powered devices relay messages for the others.
pick_when: You already have a Zigbee hub, such as Home Assistant with a USB Zigbee radio
Battery sensors spread across a house
You want it in Home Assistant through ZHA or Zigbee2MQTT
skip_when: You have no hub and do not want one
It should appear in Apple Home or Google Home without a bridge: use Matter
facts: Home Assistant suggests Zigbee channel 15, 20 or 25 "to avoid interoperability problems with Zigbee devices". Zigbee shares 2.4 GHz with Wi-Fi. Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11 overlap Zigbee channels 11 to 14, 16 to 19 and 21 to 24 (from the channel frequencies), and 15, 20 and 25 sit in the gaps. That is the US Wi-Fi plan; in Europe, Wi-Fi channel 13 overlaps Zigbee 22 to 26
No IP address; the hub translates
A coordinator is the hub's radio. Mains powered means plugged into the wall. Zigbee2MQTT and ZHA are the two ways Home Assistant runs a Zigbee network
radios.measured: LP-EM-CC2340R5 as a Zigbee light in Home Assistant: 20 of 20 commands, 95 ms median at first pairing (2026-10-05); about 5 s per command after a re-pairing two hours later; the 2026-10-16 repeat did not join. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: the radio environment. TI's example listened on channel 11 only until all channels were set. **Tag: TI example default.** That default suits a bench, not a home.

radios.name: Thread
radios.one: A low-power mesh like Zigbee, but every device gets an IPv6 address. It reaches your network through a border router.
pick_when: You have a border router already: Apple TV 4K (2nd generation, or 3rd generation Wi-Fi + Ethernet; not the Wi-Fi-only model), HomePod mini, HomePod (2nd generation), Nest Hub (2nd gen), Nest Hub Max, Nest Wifi Pro, Google TV Streamer (4K), or Home Assistant with a Connect ZBT-1 (formerly SkyConnect) or ZBT-2 running the OpenThread Border Router app
You plan to use Matter on battery devices
Battery sensors that sleep: sleepy end devices keep the radio off most of the time
skip_when: There is no border router in the house and you do not want one
Your chip is the 36 kB CC2340R52: TI's Thread device builds did not fit it, while its Bluetooth and Zigbee examples did
facts: Keep the radio on all the time, so in practice they are mains powered (plugged in). A sleepy end device keeps its radio off most of the time
IPv6, inside and outside the mesh
TI lists Thread device roles on the CC2340R53 (evaluation) and the CC27xx chips (production). On the CC2340R5 TI lists only the radio co-processor role, marked evaluation
radios.measured: Thread device builds for the LP-EM-CC2340R5 (36 kB of RAM) needed 7.5 to 23.8 kB more RAM. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: a chip limit. Only TI's configurations were built; a trimmed build might fit. They link for the 64 kB CC2340R53 and were not run.

radios.name: Matter
radios.one: Not a radio. A common language over Thread, Wi-Fi or Ethernet, so one device works with Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa, SmartThings and Home Assistant at once.
pick_when: It should work in any smart-home app, or several at once
Other people, who may not run Home Assistant, will use it
skip_when: Only you will use it, with Home Assistant: Zigbee or Bluetooth is simpler
The chip is small. TI offers Matter only on bigger wireless parts, such as the CC2755P10 (Thread, evaluation) and the CC3551E on the LP-EM-CC35X1 board (Wi-Fi, production)
facts: Thread or Wi-Fi (or Ethernet); Bluetooth LE only to set it up
A Matter controller (Apple Home, Google Home, Alexa or Home Assistant), and a border router for Thread devices
radios.measured: Not measured. TI offers no Matter build for the CC2340R5.

radios.name: Wi-Fi
radios.one: Joins your home network directly. No hub and plenty of speed, at much more power.
pick_when: It is plugged into the wall
It sends a lot of data, or talks to a web service
You want it on the network today with no hub, for example over MQTT into Home Assistant
skip_when: It runs on a small battery: staying connected alone costs about 0.4 to 1 mA
facts: 217 to 286 mA sending, 53 to 74 mA receiving, 710 µA staying connected (CC3235SF data sheet, 3.6 V). The newer CC3551E lists 430 to 975 µA connected, as target values
radios.measured: Ran on the LP-EM-CC35X1: it joins Wi-Fi and its ESPHome API answered 20 of 20 commands from a client on the board. Home Assistant adoption is not run because the test network keeps clients apart. Evidence: docs/experiments/2026-10-13-esphome-cc35xx-platform.md.

radios.name: Sub-1 GHz long range
radios.one: A lower frequency that reaches farther and passes walls better, for sensors at the far end of a garden or a farm.
pick_when: The sensor sits past where 2.4 GHz reaches. In TI's example, the same radio performance gives 292 m at 868 MHz against 233 m at 2.4 GHz, and about twice the range through an 8-inch concrete wall
It sends small readings, not much data
skip_when: A phone or a standard smart-home app should hear it directly: phones have no Sub-1 GHz radio
You read about 100 km records. Those need a slow long-range mode, high antennas and a clear line of sight
facts: A second Sub-1 GHz radio at home to receive it, such as another TI board or a BeaglePlay
radios.measured: Not measured. An LP-CC1354P10-1 is on this bench.

all_of_them: Yes, with limits. A bigger chip can run two radio stacks at once: TI lists Bluetooth together with TI 15.4 as shipping on the CC2755P10. TI's release notes say the CC23xx chips do not support two stacks at once. TI's two-radio example for the CC2755P10, Bluetooth with TI 15.4, was moved to the 36 kB CC2340R52. It did not link: 2.1 kB of RAM short even before its heap. **Tag: Unknown.** Suspected: a chip limit. Only TI's example was moved. A board can also carry two radio chips: the BeaglePlay has Wi-Fi plus a CC1352P7 for Bluetooth, Zigbee and Sub-1 GHz. Or let a hub join them: Home Assistant takes Zigbee, Thread, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi devices into one place. A CC2340R5 can also run Bluetooth or Zigbee, one at a time, by flashing different firmware.
software_intro: You can write code for a TI board with TI's own SDK or with Zephyr. On 2026-10-06, PlatformIO's board list and MicroPython's download page did not list the MSPM0 or CC23xx boards. The checks ran on an Intel Mac running macOS 15.7.9, with Zephyr 4.4.2 and GCC 12.2, TI Arm Clang 5.1.1, SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK 9.21.00.36 and MSPM0 SDK 2.11.00.07. The speed gap is mostly the compiler. With the same GCC compiler, Zephyr cost 4 to 8 percent on CoreMark, on one LP-MSPM0G3507. The C library also differs. The time-to-blink numbers below are not like for like.

rows: TI's drivers, examples and radio stacks, set up with SysConfig, TI's point-and-click tool
An open-source operating system, a Linux Foundation project, with one build tool (west) and one driver model across more than 1,000 boards

Bluetooth LE, Zigbee and proprietary 2.4 GHz, which is TI's own packet format, in the Low Power F3 SDK; Thread and Matter as separate downloads

Upstream Zephyr has no Bluetooth for the CC2340R5. **Tag: Third-party behavior.** TI's fork, its own copy of Zephyr, adds it, but on the test board its samples flashed and printed nothing. **Tag: Unknown.** The cause is not known.§Suspected cause: tool or docs. One boot setting differs from upstream, and the fork is an older Zephyr (3.7), so it is one difference among several, not proven.

software.name: TI's SDK
software.one: TI's drivers, examples and radio stacks, set up with SysConfig.
pick_when: You need a radio stack: Bluetooth, Zigbee, Thread and Matter come from TI
You want TI's examples and its graphical setup
Speed or a quick interrupt response matters: the fastest results came from TI's compiler with no operating system
skip_when: You plan to move the same code to another vendor's chips
You want one way of working across many vendors' boards
software.measured: LP-EM-CC2340R5: builds in 22 s with make and flashes in 7 s. Not like for like with the Zephyr times.

software.name: Zephyr
software.one: An open-source operating system that runs the same way on many vendors' chips.
pick_when: You may switch chips or vendors later
You want one tool and one way of working across boards
You want open source with a large community
skip_when: You need Bluetooth on the CC2340R5 today
Your board is not in upstream Zephyr: see each board's page
You need the fastest code: TI's compiler, which Zephyr does not use, was 26 percent faster than GCC at -O3 on CoreMark (LP-MSPM0G3507) and was the bigger part of the speed gap
software.measured: LP-MSPM0G3507: 3 minutes from clean to blinking with this repo's script; 9.5 minutes the first time, while the workarounds were found. LP-EM-CC2340R5: blinking 82 s after the first command, with Zephyr installed. Not like for like with the TI SDK times.

Zigbee and Wi-Fi channel frequencies: Zigbee channel n is centered at 2405 + 5 x (n - 11) MHz (IEEE 802.15.4); Wi-Fi channels 1, 6 and 11 are centered at 2412, 2437 and 2462 MHz and about 22 MHz wide
zigbee_or_thread: Both are low-power meshes on 2.4 GHz, good for battery sensors, and both work with Home Assistant. Pick Zigbee if you have a Zigbee hub or USB radio already. Pick Thread if you have a Thread border router, or want Matter on battery devices. Many Apple and Google home hubs are border routers, and Matter's low-power path is over Thread. Thread devices get IPv6 addresses; Zigbee devices need the hub to translate. On TI chips, Thread needs more memory in TI's builds: on the 36 kB CC2340R52 Thread device builds did not fit and Zigbee did.
next: Pick a board: open the [Hardware options page](hardware.html?need=zigbee) and press the need you chose. Hit an error: the LP-EM-CC2340R5 FAQ lists each one with its cause. Not measured: Wi-Fi, Sub-1 GHz, Matter, indoor range and battery life.
answers_intro: Three common questions. Each answer gives the requirement, a configuration that ran, what limits it, and what no row establishes. Every number in the tables is read from the results store when the page is built. A constraint that is not measured names the experiment that would decide it, and until then the answer is a candidate. Terms: ZHA is Home Assistant's Zigbee integration. LQI and RSSI are the link quality and signal strength a radio reports. NNC is TI's neural network compiler. EnergyTrace is the current meter in TI's debug probe. FOC is field-oriented control, the usual motor-control math. The TMU is the C2000's hardware for sine, cosine and division.

answers.question: A Zigbee light or switch in Home Assistant: which TI board, and whether it responds fast enough
answers.bottom_line: LP-EM-CC2340R5 with TI's onoff_light example: 20 of 20 commands landed at a 95 ms median on first pairing (2026-10-05), but about 5 s after a re-pairing, and the 2026-10-16 repeat did not join Home Assistant at all (cause open). RAM is tight, 799 B free in the router build.
answers.requirement: A device that joins an existing Zigbee network run by Home Assistant (ZHA) and acts on a command within about a second.
answers.candidate: LP-EM-CC2340R5 with TI's onoff_light example from the SimpleLink Low Power F3 SDK, built as a router, plus the LP-XDS110ET debugger to program it.
answers.why: It joined ZHA (Home Assistant's own Zigbee integration) 37 s after the flash finished, and 20 of 20 on/off commands from Home Assistant landed, median 95 ms, read from Home Assistant's own state. That meets the requirement on the first pairing. After a re-pairing two hours later the median was about 5 s, which does not, so the one-second part is met once and missed once. A repeat on 2026-10-16 did not join Home Assistant in four tries; until a new run passes, this is a record of one run, not a tested route.
answers.limit: RAM, and the link. The router image leaves 799 B of the chip's 36 kB free, so there is almost no room for your own code in that build; the end-device image leaves 6.4 kB. The 5 s medians came with a weaker link (LQI, the link quality the radio reports, 36 to 48 against 60 at first). Cause unknown (suspected: radio environment).

answers.question: A small on-chip classifier under 5 ms per answer on a coin-cell budget: whether the MSPM0G5187's NPU reaches it
answers.bottom_line: LP-MSPM0G5187: 2.12 ms per answer on the NPU against a 5 ms budget, model call only. Accuracy on a new day is 40.2 percent balanced, and coin-cell life is unmeasured.
answers.requirement: A 4-class classifier on 4 sensor channels by 32 samples, answered in under 5 ms, in a few kB of flash and RAM, with the model's accuracy known.
answers.candidate: LP-MSPM0G5187 with the 8.5k-parameter occupancy model compiled by TI's NNC for the NPU, at 80 MHz.
answers.why: The answer takes 2.12 ms on the NPU (the chip's neural processing unit) at 80 MHz, so the 5 ms budget is met twice over. The model objects take 14.0 kB of flash and 1.4 kB of RAM. The 20 stored test vectors give the same class on the board as on the Mac, so the port is right. For scale: TI's own CPU build of the same model (NNC, TI's neural network compiler) takes 45.64 ms, 21.6 times longer, and the fastest plain C build 35.27 ms; that last pair is not like for like because the plain C time also includes input quantization.
answers.limit: What the model knows, not the chip. Balanced accuracy is the average of how often each class is caught. On a day the model never trained on it is 87.7 percent accurate overall but calls 159 of 170 three-person windows empty, a balanced accuracy of 40.2 percent; the 90.9 percent figure comes from a same-day split. And the time is the model call only: no sensor read, no sleep or wake, so it is not a pipeline latency.

answers.question: A 50 kHz motor-control loop: which board keeps up, and how much of the period is left
answers.bottom_line: LAUNCHXL-F2800137: one field-oriented control step takes 2.4 us, about 12 percent of the 20 us period at 50 kHz. It is one step on a fixed input; it does not drive a motor.
answers.requirement: A PWM-triggered loop (ADC sample, one field-oriented control step, new PWM value) that completes well inside a 20 us period, with the CPU time it takes known.
answers.candidate: LAUNCHXL-F2800137 (TMS320F2800137 at 120 MHz) with the TMU build of a control-loop harness, code in RAM.
answers.why: Trigger to new PWM value takes 2.4 us mean (2.33 to 2.42 us over 1,000 interrupts) with the TMU, the chip's hardware for sine, cosine and division, in one field-oriented control (FOC) step. At 50 kHz the period is 20 us, so the loop uses about 12 percent of it. The loop still updates every period up to 336 kHz, and at 100 kHz it takes 26.4 percent of the CPU.
answers.limit: This is one FOC step on a fixed input, not a motor: no current sensing chain, no observer, no fault handling, no communications. The 336 kHz figure is where the harness stops updating in time; your loop has more in it.
